name: AdaptHealth Corp.
as_of: 2026-08-04 post-print, IBKR conid 391048323, last 6.73 / bid 6.72 / ask 6.73, prior close 10.83, -37.86%, intraday low 6.14, volume 13.4x ADV
classification: DERAILMENT / LEVERED-STUB — EBITDA-multiple cheapness is an artifact of using EBITDA for a business whose maintenance capex equals its EBITDA. Confirms the triage NO.
plan: NO POSITION. Not an entry, not a ladder, not an armed gate. The shock hit the value pillar itself (margin structure and cash conversion), so the response-taxonomy answer is a size cut to zero, not a price gate. Re-court only if BOTH legs fire: (1) PRICE below $5.00 (where the equity is supported on a free-cash-flow lens rather than an EBITDA lens), AND (2) EVIDENCE — one clean quarter of Q3-2026 capex at or under $90M with the FY26 free-cash-flow guide of $80-120M reaffirmed. Price alone is not sufficient; the bear leg is a further EBITDA decline, and buying a falling EBITDA at a lower multiple is how this name has destroyed capital for three consecutive years. The peer set closes the door on the cheapness argument: AHCO now trades at 5.4-5.7x against VMD at 5.5-6.0x and Accendra at 5.6-5.9x, and the only completed 2026 HME take-private (Quipt) cleared at 4.2x — below spot. If the desk wants HME exposure at all, the cleaner expression is the credit, not the equity: the 4.625% notes due Aug-2029 sit ahead of a $244M tax-receivable obligation and $1.39B of book equity.
catalyst: Q3-2026 print expected early November 2026 (exact date UNVERIFIABLE) — the single decisive datapoint is Q3 capex, which must fall to roughly $65-85M/qtr from $166.2M in Q2 for the FY26 free-cash-flow guide to hold. Q3 goodwill impairment on Sleep Health is close to a formality: the 6/30 impairment test that wrote down Respiratory and Wellness was run BEFORE the 38% break, Sleep still carries $1.61B of unimpaired goodwill, total goodwill of $2.37B is 2.6x the market cap, and management's own stated trigger is a sustained decline in market capitalization. Diabetes Health sale to Cardinal Health (RGH Enterprises) for $235M closes Q1-2027 subject to HSR — NOT in 2026, so there is no near-term deleveraging. 12/31/2026 covenant certificate is the first hard test of the 3.50x maintenance covenant.

FY26 adjusted EBITDA guide cut again below $490M (would be the third cut in twelve months and puts the 3.50x covenant in play)
Any amendment, waiver or covenant relief request on the 2026 Credit Agreement
Continuing-operations adjusted EBITDA tracking below roughly $465M annualized — the level at which the 3.50x total-leverage covenant binds once Diabetes leaves the trailing twelve months
Diabetes Health sale terminated, repriced, or delayed past Q2-2027 on HSR

A second capitated contract (Humana OneHome, 478,000 members) disclosed as margin-dilutive on the Q3 or Q4 call — that converts the $55M West Coast hit from a one-contract problem into a business-model problem

Material quantification of the July 2026 cybersecurity incident (Item 1.05) — patient management systems and an insurance-billing password file were exfiltrated; the financial impact is still unquantified

Index membership and therefore any mechanical forced-selling — could not be sourced. Note that at a $918M market cap there is no size-driven S&P/Russell deletion mechanic in play regardless, and the next Russell reconstitution is June 2027.

EVIDENCE-GRADE CAVEAT on the supply-chain leg: the Philips Respironics US re-entry detail and the industry-wide 2026 DME cost-inflation quantification were covered at headline level only (a delegated thread stalled). Treat both as PLAUSIBLE, not CONFIRMED. court_record.ruling: DERAILMENT, not de-rate. Estimates fell and the multiple followed. Fails the quality leg of the court frame outright.
seed_corrections: REFUTED — 'approximately $570M market cap.' Actual 136,344,196 shares outstanding as of 2026-07-31 (10-Q cover) at $6.73 = $918M. Independently corroborated at $913M by the broken-print radar. The error understates the equity by ~61% and is what made the stub look cheap.

REFUTED — 'stack = credit facility + 5.125% 2030 notes.' There are also $500M of 4.625% Senior Notes due August 2029. Confirmed tranches post the August-3 redemption of the 2028s: $500M 4.625% 2029 + $600M 5.125% 2030 + $650M term loans + $150M revolver = $1,900M.

REFUTED — 'NO 2027-28 maturity wall' is true only as stated. The 2026 Credit Facility's April-2031 stated maturity SPRINGS to 91 days before the 4.625% 2029 notes (roughly May 2029) if more than $150M of those notes remain outstanding. $500M is outstanding. So ~$800M of bank debt springs to 2029 unless the 2029 notes are refinanced first — and refinancing 4.625% paper in today's market adds roughly $20-25M/yr of interest.

CORRECTED — 'net loss $145.3M.' The press-release highlight labels $145.3M as 'net loss attributable to AdaptHealth Corp.' but the income statement shows $133.9M. The $145.3M figure is the CONTINUING-operations attributable loss. The mislabel makes the loss look larger, not smaller — anti-promotional, so no masking finding, but the two numbers are not interchangeable.

CORRECTED — the '2021 deja-vu' framing does not survive the filings. 2021-22 was two modest ~4% EBITDA guide cuts, not a cut-string; the destruction was the April-2021 Luke McGee tax-fraud charge and the 2023 diabetes-billing year (Allegheny County ERS class action, settled $35.0M, dismissed with prejudice 2026-06-10). More importantly the inheritance thesis is inverted — see below.

REFUTED — 'is the current team the cleanup crew hitting inherited contracts?' No. The West Coast capitated contract was entered in Q3-2025, roughly fifteen months into Suzanne Foster's tenure (CEO since May 2024), and she celebrated it in February 2026 as 'the largest capitated contract in the industry's history.' This is the current team's own underwriting failure, not inherited damage. CFO Jason Clemens is the one continuity officer (since 2020, through AeroCare and the class-period). The COO hired in 2024 was terminated without cause 2026-05-04 after ~20 months.

MISLEADING — 'revenue FINE ($740.3M +12.7%, organic +15.9%).' The revenue growth IS the problem. Per MD&A, the growth in BOTH Sleep Health and Respiratory Health is attributed primarily to 'a capitated revenue contract that was entered into in the third quarter of 2025' — the same contract carrying the $55M EBITDA hit. And AHCO's own published definition of organic revenue explicitly counts patient books bought from prior providers as organic: it excludes acquisitions generally but carves back in 'the acquisition of assets from previous providers to facilitate the transition of patients related to newly awarded at-risk capitated contracts, since the revenue related to these agreements is earned organically.' The company spent $127.4M of cash on business acquisitions in H1 and reported the resulting revenue as 15.9% ORGANIC growth.

SOFTENED — my own first-pass 'negative selection' finding. Diabetes Health was indeed the low-capex asset (1.7% vs 19.9%), but CY2026 rulemaking bundled CGMs/insulin pumps into monthly rental and Round 2028 competitive bidding targets exactly that book. Selling it to Cardinal ahead of that is defensible portfolio management, not purely selling the crown jewel. The retained sleep/respiratory book faces no equivalent rate action.
court_record.mode_b_lead: Adjusted EBITDA is the wrong metric for this business and its cheapness is an artifact. Patient-equipment depreciation is not an accounting abstraction here — it is the recurring cost of the equipment AdaptHealth must buy to hold a patient. Q2-2026: adjusted EBITDA $132.0M against D&A of $114.8M and interest of $26.2M, so economic earnings were NEGATIVE $9.0M, versus POSITIVE $22.0M a year ago. Segment level, adjusted EBITDA less patient-equipment depreciation: Sleep Health $21.1M (from $35.1M, -40%); Respiratory Health $15.0M (flat); Wellness at Home NEGATIVE $10.9M (from -$1.1M) on 21% of revenue. Two of three segments are deteriorating and Wellness is structurally loss-making after the cost of its own equipment. On the only metric that matters to a levered equity — free cash flow — the stub trades at roughly 28x the FY26 consolidated guide midpoint and 40x+ on continuing operations, not the 5.2x that EV/EBITDA advertises.

That is real convexity, but the strike is close: HME comps have traded through 4x in bad tape, so the zero is a live outcome rather than a theoretical one, and the underlying — EBITDA — is the thing management just proved it cannot forecast.

covenant_reality.source: 2026 Credit Agreement, Section 8.8, filed as an exhibit to the 2026-04-13 8-K (conformedsignaturescredita.htm). Read directly, not inferred.
covenant_reality.max_total_leverage: 3.50:1.0, stepping up to 4.00:1.0 for only four quarters following a Permitted Acquisition with total consideration of $100M or more
covenant_reality.type: MAINTENANCE covenant tested every fiscal quarter — not an incurrence test
covenant_reality.definitions: Consolidated Total Leverage Ratio = Consolidated Funded Indebtedness (net of unrestricted cash, capped at $300M) / trailing-four-quarter Consolidated EBITDA. Addbacks for non-recurring charges, restructuring and run-rate cost savings are capped in aggregate at 25% of Consolidated EBITDA.
covenant_reality.anchor: The 10-Q discloses $265.7M of revolver capacity available while remaining covenant-compliant at 6/30/26 — which equals exactly the undrawn commitment ($450M less $150M drawn less $34.3M of letters of credit), implying trailing covenant EBITDA of at least ~$629M at 6/30/26 and therefore that covenant addbacks run only ~4% above reported adjusted EBITDA. Modest addbacks, so the covenant cannot be inflated away.
covenant_reality.test_12_31_2026: Diabetes is still owned (sale closes Q1-2027), so its EBITDA still counts. Estimated covenant EBITDA ~$630M against net funded debt ~$1,929M = ~3.06x versus the 3.50x limit. Breach requires covenant EBITDA below ~$551M — a further ~12.5% miss.
covenant_reality.test_post_close_2027: Once Diabetes leaves the trailing twelve months and $218M of net proceeds pay down debt, the ratio is roughly neutral at ~3.06x. The covenant binds at roughly $465M of continuing adjusted EBITDA — about 8-9% below the guide midpoint.
covenant_reality.interest_coverage_read: ~6.3x against a 3.00x floor. Not the binding constraint.
covenant_reality.verdict: The seed's '~3.65x versus no wall' framing is wrong in both directions: it uses the continuing-operations denominator (which overstates covenant leverage, since Diabetes still counts until Q1-2027) while missing that the covenant is a hard 3.50x maintenance test. Actual headroom is ~0.44 turns / ~12.5% of EBITDA at the 12/31/26 test, narrowing to ~8-9% once Diabetes is gone. Not imminent — but thin for a management team with a fresh 14% operational forecast error, and covenant risk in 2027 is materially higher than the seed implies.

court_record.the_hinge_finding: FY2025 actuals reframe everything. FY25 adjusted EBITDA was $616.7M, DOWN 10.5% from FY24's $688.7M, and FY25 already carried a $128.0M goodwill impairment — so 2026's $144.2M is the SECOND consecutive year of impairment. In February 2026, off that declining base, management guided FY26 to $680-730M (up 10-18%) and wrote that 'the underlying earnings power of the business remains intact' — while in the same release disclosing that Q4-2025 already absorbed 'over $10 million of strategic investments to accelerate onboarding the new capitated contract.' The cost overrun on that contract was therefore visible in Q4-2025 and was characterized as a discrete strategic investment. Six months later the same contract is a $55M structural drag and the total-company FY26 outlook (~$605M including Diabetes) is BELOW the FY25 base. Trajectory: FY24 $688.7M, FY25 $616.7M, FY26E ~$605M — three consecutive years of EBITDA decline while revenue compounds. That is the takeaway-versus-data divergence, and it is what the market repriced.
court_record.capitation_read: The 10-Q does not disclose capitated revenue as a percentage of total — the top gap. What IS confirmed: the Q3-2025 capitated contract is the primary named driver of revenue growth in both Sleep Health and Respiratory Health; management signed a SECOND capitated agreement (Humana OneHome, ~478,000 members transitioned) during the quarter in which the first one was destroying margin; gross patient medical equipment rose from $907.7M to $1,077.4M in six months (+18.7%) and delivery vehicles from $14.5M to $34.4M (+137%), which is a fleet-and-equipment buildout, not a working-capital wiggle; and H1 capex of $287.5M understates true capex by a further ~$22M of increased unpaid-equipment accrual ($81.7M vs $59.2M). Capitation in HME means fixed per-member revenue against AHCO-borne utilization risk, funded by front-loaded equipment purchases depreciated over five years. The economics only work if utilization comes in under the bid — and AHCO has now missed that bid on its first large contract by $55M.
court_record.negative_selection: The divestiture sells the wrong asset. Diabetes Health generated $294.4M of H1 revenue on $5.0M of capex — 1.7% capex intensity — versus 19.9% for continuing operations. Post-close, AdaptHealth's capital intensity RISES. Cardinal Health (RGH Enterprises) is paying $235M against roughly $77-88M of annualized unallocated EBITDA as presented in discontinued operations, i.e. ~2.7-3.0x, or ~5.9x on the $40M fully-allocated basis implied by the company's own guide bridge. That is the cleanest available HME transaction comp and it prices AT OR BELOW where the remaining, more capital-hungry stub trades (5.2x pro forma). The buyer of the good asset is paying less than the market is being asked to pay for the bad one.
court_record.impairment_signal: The impairment hit Respiratory Health ($79.1M) and Wellness at Home ($65.1M, 36% of that unit's goodwill). Respiratory's reported Q2 margin EXPANDED (26.6% to 27.3%) and its EBITDA rose 17.2% — yet its reporting-unit fair value fell below carrying value. That means management's forward projections for Respiratory were cut hard in a way the segment P&L does not show. The charge is honest disclosure, but it discloses a forecast cut the reported trend conceals. Separately, Sleep Health's $1.61B of goodwill survived a test run as of 6/30 — before the 38% break — against a market cap that is now $918M and total goodwill of $2.37B.
court_record.positioning_and_discovery: CROWDED-LONG UNWIND, day 1 — not an undiscovered dislocation. The stock ran from $8.35 in February to a $13.43 high in early July (+58%) and Jefferies upgraded to Buy on 2026-07-21, with Truist reiterating Buy and Canaccord maintaining Buy/$16 the same day — fourteen days before a 28% guide cut. Short interest is only 7.79% of float at 4.96 days to cover, so there is no squeeze fuel; the 13.4x-ADV volume on the break is long capitulation, and de-crowding of a consensus-long small-cap takes weeks, not one session. No mechanical forced selling identified. The one genuinely clean contrary signal: One Equity Partners bought 2,046,691 shares in the open market in March 2026 at $9.73-9.94 (~$20.0M, taking it to 12.0% with two board seats), the Chairman bought 8,000 at $8.96 and the CLO 5,000 at $8.91, and there was zero discretionary insider selling all year. That signal is real but stale by five months and roughly 35%, and none of it post-dates the capitated deterioration.
court_record.additional_risk_not_in_seed: 2026-07-02 Item 1.05 material cybersecurity incident. A threat actor reached internal patient management systems and document storage via social engineering of a third-party contractor session and exfiltrated a stored password file tied to insurance billing plus PII/PHI. No SSNs or payment data. Financial impact explicitly not yet quantifiable — an unbounded HIPAA/remediation/litigation tail on a business with no free cash flow to absorb it. Also open: a North Carolina debt-collection class action asserting classes up to ~130,000 patients, and a Holzer & Holzer securities investigation opened on the day of the break.

peer_comp_set.bull_leg_damage: The takeout leg weakens on two counts: Rotech died on HSR, so in-market strategic consolidation carries real antitrust risk; and the only completed 2026 HME take-private cleared at 4.2x — at or BELOW where AHCO already trades. A sponsor bid is not an automatic premium here.
peer_comp_set.sector_read: VMD's adjusted-EBITDA margin fell 23.9% (Q4-25) to 19.0% (Q1-26) to 17.6% (Q2-26) on +24% revenue, and VMD fell 15.8% the same session. HME cost pressure is SECTOR-WIDE. That partly exonerates AHCO management — but it cuts against the bull, because it reframes the margin hit as industry cost inflation rather than a transitory AHCO onboarding cost.
peer_comp_set.distress_template: Accendra Health announced a >$1.5B distressed 'balance sheet optimization' with creditors on 2026-05-11 with Q1-26 adjusted EBITDA of $58.4M vs $96.0M (-39%). That is the live template for what a levered HME equity does when EBITDA declines into its leverage — it is what the AHCO bear leg looks like in practice, not a theoretical construct.

court_record.pass_through_verdict: RESOLVED AGAINST THE BULL, from primary sources. Medicare DMEPOS rates are administratively fixed by fee schedule / single payment amounts (42 CFR 414.210) — there is no cost-plus or rate-relief mechanism, and capitated PMPM contracts are strictly worse. AHCO's own FY25 10-K concedes reliance on 'two to three suppliers for each of its product categories' and that tariffs/excise taxes 'could be passed on to customers, such as AdaptHealth,' while the 10-Q concedes 'it is not certain whether AdaptHealth would be able to pass increased costs onto customers.' Philips Respironics has still not returned as a full US CPAP competitor (only a limited DreamStation BiPAP re-entry, Mar-2026), so the supplier retains oligopoly pricing power. CONCLUSION: the $30M manufacturer price increase is STRUCTURAL, not one-time. Roughly a third of the $100M operational guide cut is therefore permanent unless renegotiated with the manufacturer. The manufacturer's identity is still unconfirmed — ResMed is trade-press suspicion only, though RMD's Q3-FY26 non-GAAP gross margin rose 290bps to 62.8% with no pricing commentary, which is consistent with but does not prove it.
court_record.reimbursement_clean_bill: A genuine BULL point and a correction to my negative-selection finding. There is NO 2026-27 Medicare rate cliff for the sleep/respiratory book: the 75/25 blended rate already expired 12/31/2023 (a 2024 event, not a pending catalyst); Round 2028 competitive bidding covers CGMs, insulin pumps, catheters, ostomy, urological and braces but EXCLUDES CPAP, oxygen and ventilators entirely; the CY2027 HH PPS proposed rule (91 FR 41216) contains no DMEPOS rate cut; and the nationwide 6-month DMEPOS enrollment moratorium effective 2026-02-27 is incumbent-favorable. Critically, the CY2026 final rule moved CGMs and insulin pumps to bundled monthly rental and set SPA methodology at the 75th percentile of winning bids — so selling Diabetes Health to Cardinal three weeks before this print DODGED the CGM bidding pincer. My 'negative selection' finding must be softened: the asset sold was the higher-quality one on capex intensity, but its regulatory outlook was deteriorating in a way the retained book's is not. The real forward volume risk is Medicaid attrition from 1/1/2027 under OBBBA work requirements and 6-month redeterminations.

edge_explainer: The triage NO is CONFIRMED, and the deep-value read fails on a corrected fact before it fails on judgment: the market cap is $918M, not the $570M in the seed (136,344,196 shares from the 10-Q cover at a tape-verified $6.73). That single correction moves pro-forma EV/EBITDA from apparently distressed to roughly 5.2x — a fair-to-full HME multiple, not a dislocated one, and above the ~2.7-5.9x Cardinal Health is paying for AdaptHealth's own best asset. The deeper objection is that EV/EBITDA is the wrong lens here. Patient-equipment depreciation is this company's cost of goods: in Q2, adjusted EBITDA of $132.0M against $114.8M of D&A and $26.2M of interest produced NEGATIVE $9.0M of economic earnings versus positive $22.0M a year earlier, and Wellness at Home is now loss-making after the cost of its own equipment. On free cash flow — the only metric a levered equity can service debt with — the stub trades at ~28x the FY26 consolidated guide and 40x+ on continuing operations, and H1 free cash flow was NEGATIVE $48.4M against positive $73.3M. Three things the seed missed sharpen this. First, FY25 adjusted EBITDA was already down 10.5% to $616.7M with a $128M impairment, and management still guided FY26 up 10-18% while disclosing that the capitated contract had already consumed 'over $10 million' in Q4-2025 — so this is the third consecutive year of EBITDA decline and the second consecutive impairment, not a first stumble. Second, the leverage covenant is a hard 3.50x MAINTENANCE test with a 3.00x interest-coverage floor, read directly from Section 8.8 of the April-2026 credit agreement; headroom is ~12.5% of EBITDA at the 12/31/26 test and ~8-9% once Diabetes leaves the trailing twelve months, and the $235M of proceeds do not arrive until Q1-2027 because of HSR. Third, the failing contract was signed by the CURRENT team in Q3-2025 and celebrated by the CEO in February 2026 as 'the largest capitated contract in the industry's history' — the cleanup-crew defense is inverted, and management signed a SECOND capitated deal (Humana OneHome, 478,000 members) during the quarter the first one blew up. The honesty finding is the organic-growth framing: AHCO's own published definition counts patient books purchased from prior providers as ORGANIC revenue, so $127.4M of H1 acquisition cash plus $287.5M of capex bought 15.9% 'organic' growth that delivered LOWER EBITDA dollars and $122M less free cash flow than the prior year. Revenue is not fine; the revenue growth is the problem. The peer lane then closed the remaining gap: AHCO's 38% crash re-rated it INTO the HME band (5.4-5.7x vs VMD 5.5-6.0x and Accendra Health 5.6-5.9x), not to a discount; the only completed 2026 HME take-private, Quipt at 4.2x, cleared BELOW spot; the Rotech deal died on FTC antitrust rather than price, which impairs the strategic-takeout leg; VMD's own margin fell 23.9% to 17.6% over three quarters on +24% revenue, reframing AHCO's margin hit as sector-wide cost inflation rather than a transitory onboarding cost; Accendra Health is already in a >$1.5B distressed creditor negotiation with EBITDA down 39%, which is the live template for the bear leg; and Medicare DMEPOS rates are administratively fixed under 42 CFR 414.210 with no pass-through mechanism, making the $30M supplier increase STRUCTURAL rather than one-time. The one genuine offset is that there is no 2026-27 rate cliff for the retained sleep/respiratory book and the Diabetes sale dodged the CY2026 CGM bundling and Round 2028 bidding — so the divestiture is better-timed than a pure negative-selection read allows. Net of all of it, expected fair value $6.77 against $6.73 is +0.6% — no edge at all for a security with a 35%-probability bear leg that loses roughly half, an unquantified cyber liability, a $244M tax-receivable claim ahead of the equity that appears in no sell-side bridge, and a credit facility whose stated 2031 maturity springs to 2029 against the $500M of 4.625% notes. Not a de-rate on stable estimates. Derailment.

frozen_call_proposals.bar: At the Q3-2026 print: purchases of equipment and other fixed assets are $90M or less for the quarter AND the FY26 free-cash-flow guide of $80-120M is reaffirmed or raised (not lowered or withdrawn).
frozen_call_proposals.why_this_bar: This is the load-bearing bull assumption reduced to one observable line. H1 free cash flow was -$48.4M, so the FY26 guide requires H2 free cash flow of +$128M to +$168M, which requires H2 capex of roughly $130-170M against $166.2M in Q2 alone and $287.5M in H1. Management says the West Coast contract is at run-rate, but Humana OneHome's 478,000 members transitioned during the period and capitated onboarding is equipment-funded. FY25 free cash flow was H2-weighted (66%), which is the honest argument for the bull — but H2-25 capex was $198.1M and this needs materially less while onboarding a second contract.

frozen_call_proposals.why_this_bar: Deliberately a high-probability call, to test whether the court is over-weighting covenant risk. My own math says the 12/31/26 test clears at ~3.06x versus the 3.50x limit and needs a further ~12.5% EBITDA miss to breach. If this resolves NO, the court under-weighted the covenant; if it resolves YES, the covenant was correctly identified as a 2027 issue rather than a 2026 one.

four_idea_frame.idea_1_what_the_market_believes: A leveraged HME roll-up cut guidance 28% and printed a goodwill impairment; the equity is a broken stub and was sold indiscriminately at 13.4x average volume.
four_idea_frame.idea_2_what_is_actually_true: Revenue is compounding and two of the three cited EBITDA drivers are self-inflicted and arguably transitional; the sponsor bought $20M in the open market five months ago; and pro-forma EV/EBITDA of ~5.2x is not obviously expensive against HME M&A at 6-7.5x.
four_idea_frame.idea_3_what_that_misses: Adjusted EBITDA approximately equals maintenance capex in this business, so the EBITDA multiple is not a valuation — it is a category error. Economic earnings (EBITDA less D&A less interest) are NEGATIVE $9M/quarter and were positive $22M a year ago; FY26 will be the third consecutive year of EBITDA decline and the second consecutive goodwill impairment; and the divestiture sells the 1.7%-capex-intensity asset while keeping the 20%-capex-intensity one, at a price (2.7-5.9x) below where the remainder trades.
four_idea_frame.idea_4_the_trade: None. The correct expression of a correct view here is no position. The +8.3% expected edge does not pay for a 35% bear leg at roughly -48%, a hard 3.50x maintenance covenant with single-digit percentage headroom post-close, a $244M tax-receivable claim ahead of the equity, and an unquantified July cybersecurity liability. Re-court on price below $5.00 AND one clean quarter of capex discipline — both, not either.
